text: This guide covers two things, from US government sources: making water safe to drink (EPA and Ready.gov) and making a fire (the US Army survival manual, FM 21-76). It is not medical advice. If someone is hurt, poisoned or in danger, call your local emergency number first.

Boiling makes water safe from germs. Bring it to a rolling boil for at least one minute; above 5,000 feet (1,000 meters), boil it for three minutes. If the water is cloudy, let it settle and filter it through a clean cloth, paper towel or coffee filter first. Let it cool naturally and store it in clean, covered containers. A pinch of salt per quart or liter, or pouring it between clean containers, improves the flat taste. [EPA, Emergency Disinfection of Drinking Water, updated Feb 24, 2026]

For disinfecting water, use regular, unscented chlorine bleach labeled for disinfection, with 6% or 8.25% sodium hypochlorite. Never use scented or color-safe bleach, or bleach with added cleaners. Use fresh bleach, stored at room temperature for less than a year, and a clean dropper. [EPA, Emergency Disinfection of Drinking Water, updated Feb 24, 2026]

Bleach per amount of water (6% bleach / 8.25% bleach): 1 quart or liter: 2 drops / 2 drops. 1 gallon: 8 drops / 6 drops. 2 gallons: 16 drops (1/4 teaspoon) / 12 drops (1/8 teaspoon). 4 gallons: 1/3 teaspoon / 1/4 teaspoon. 8 gallons: 2/3 teaspoon / 1/2 teaspoon. Double the amount if the water is cloudy, colored or very cold. [EPA, Emergency Disinfection of Drinking Water, updated Feb 24, 2026] Ready.gov gives the same dose as 1/8 teaspoon per gallon of 5.25–6% bleach. [Ready.gov, Water]

After adding bleach, stir and let the water stand for 30 minutes. It should smell slightly of chlorine. If it doesn't, repeat the dose and wait another 15 minutes. If the chlorine taste is strong, pour it between clean containers and let it stand a few hours. [EPA, Emergency Disinfection of Drinking Water, updated Feb 24, 2026] If it still has no chlorine smell after the second dose, throw it out and find another source. [Ready.gov, Water]

Iodine: add five drops of 2% tincture of iodine per quart or liter (ten if the water is cloudy or colored), stir, and let it stand at least 30 minutes. Disinfection tablets (chlorine, iodine or chlorine dioxide) differ in strength, so follow the product label. [EPA, Emergency Disinfection of Drinking Water, updated Feb 24, 2026] Ready.gov does not recommend iodine, or camping treatment products whose only active ingredient is not 5.25–6% sodium hypochlorite. [Ready.gov, Water]

Boiling and disinfecting kill germs, but they do not remove heavy metals, salts or most other chemicals. [EPA, Emergency Disinfection of Drinking Water, updated Feb 24, 2026] Distillation does: fill a pot halfway with water, tie a cup to the lid's handle so it hangs upright without touching the water, and boil for 20 minutes. The water that drips from the lid into the cup is distilled. [Ready.gov, Water]

Cloudy water: let the particles settle, or strain the water through coffee filters or layers of clean cloth, then boil or disinfect it. With bleach, cloudy, colored or very cold water needs double the dose. [Ready.gov, Water] [EPA, Emergency Disinfection of Drinking Water, updated Feb 24, 2026]

Store at least one gallon of water per person per day for several days, for drinking and sanitation. A normally active person needs about three quarters of a gallon of fluid a day. Children, nursing mothers, sick people and anyone in very hot weather may need more; in heat, needs can double. Don't ration drinking water unless authorities tell you to. [Ready.gov, Water]

Buy commercially bottled water and keep it in its sealed container in a cool, dark place. For your own containers, use food-grade ones: wash them with dish soap, then sanitize them with one teaspoon of unscented liquid household bleach per quart of water. Replace water that isn't commercially bottled every six months. [Ready.gov, Water]

Treat water of uncertain quality before you drink it, cook with it, wash dishes, brush your teeth or make ice. Cloudy tap water and water from streams or ponds count as suspicious. Don't drink carbonated, caffeinated or alcoholic drinks instead of water: they dehydrate you. [Ready.gov, Water]

A fire needs air, heat and fuel; take any one away and it goes out. Solid fuel doesn't burn directly: heat turns it into gas, which burns when it mixes with oxygen. Getting the balance of the three right comes with practice. [US Army FM 21-76, Survival, ch. 7 Firecraft]

Choose a spot that is dry, sheltered from the wind, close to fuel, and placed so the heat goes where you want it. In brush or woods, clear the brush and scrape the surface soil away in a circle at least 1 meter (3 feet) across. Logs or rocks around the fire reflect heat and cut sparks and wind, but leave it enough air. Never use wet or porous rocks: they can explode when heated. [US Army FM 21-76, Survival, ch. 7 Firecraft]

A Dakota fire hole hides the fire and works well for cooking: dig a hole for the fire, dig a larger connecting air hole on the upwind side, and build the fire in the first hole. On snow, build a platform: lay several green logs side by side, then add one or two more layers, each crossing the one below. [US Army FM 21-76, Survival, ch. 7 Firecraft]

You need three materials. Tinder: very dry material that catches from a spark; char cloth (cotton heated until black but not burning, then kept airtight), alcohol pads or petroleum-jelly gauze work well. Kindling: dry, readily burning pieces you add to burning tinder to raise the heat. Fuel: larger material that burns slowly and steadily once lit. [US Army FM 21-76, Survival, ch. 7 Firecraft]

Tepee: stand kindling sticks in a cone over the tinder and light the center; as the outside burns, it falls inward and feeds the fire, and it burns even with wet wood. Lean-to: push a green stick into the ground at about 30 degrees, pointing into the wind, put tinder under it, lean kindling against it, and add more kindling as it catches. [US Army FM 21-76, Survival, ch. 7 Firecraft]

Cross-ditch: scratch a cross about 30 cm (12 in) across and 7.5 cm (3 in) deep, put a large wad of tinder in the center and build a kindling pyramid above it; the ditch draws air under the tinder. Pyramid: lay two small logs side by side, then layers of smaller logs, each crossing the one below; light a fire on top and it burns downward, needing little tending overnight. [US Army FM 21-76, Survival, ch. 7 Firecraft]

Light the fire from the upwind side. Matches: keep waterproof matches in a waterproof container with a reliable striker. Lens: on a bright, sunny day, focus sunlight through a magnifier or a lens from binoculars or a camera onto the tinder until it smolders, then blow it into flame. Metal match: lay a dry leaf under the tinder, hold the metal match on it and scrape a knife down it to throw sparks onto the tinder. [US Army FM 21-76, Survival, ch. 7 Firecraft]

Flint and steel: strike a hard, sharp-edged rock with carbon steel to throw sparks onto the tinder. Stainless steel won't make a good spark. It takes a loose wrist and practice. When the tinder catches a spark, blow on it gently. [US Army FM 21-76, Survival, ch. 7 Firecraft]

Bow and drill parts: a hand socket with a small hollow, a straight, seasoned hardwood drill about 2 cm (3/4 in) thick and 25 cm (10 in) long, a seasoned softwood board about 2.5 cm (1 in) thick and 10 cm (4 in) wide with a hollow and a V-shaped notch beside it, and a bow of springy green wood with a tight string. Put tinder under the notch, hold the board with your foot, loop the bowstring over the drill, set the drill in the hollow, press down on the socket and saw the bow. When it spins smoothly, press harder and go faster. [US Army FM 21-76, Survival, ch. 7 Firecraft]

Bow and drill tips: use seasoned, non-aromatic hardwood if you can; don't use wood lying on the ground; dry damp wood near a fire before you need it; once the tinder smolders, blow it into flame; bank the fire to keep coals alive overnight. [US Army FM 21-76, Survival, ch. 7 Firecraft]

Fire-plow: cut a straight groove in a softwood base, then push the blunt tip of a hardwood shaft up and down the groove. The rubbing makes small wood particles, and pressing harder on each stroke heats them until they ignite. [US Army FM 21-76, Survival, ch. 7 Firecraft]

A fire in a shelter can cause burns and carbon monoxide poisoning. Never use wet or porous rocks around a fire: they can explode. Make sure the fire is completely out before you leave. [US Army FM 21-76, Survival, ch. 7 Firecraft]
